newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish drivers continue strike, disruption spreads.
newsitem.headline: Danish drivers continue strike, disruption spreads.

text.p: Militant Danish truckers voted on Thursday to continue a four-day-old blockade of seaports and frontier crossings which has already disrupted domestic and European commerce.
"We have chosen to continue our action for the time being," drivers' spokesman Ole Prusse told Reuters from protest headquarters at the Padborg border crossing to Germany.

"We have sent a couple of our people to parliament in Copenhagen to explain our case. I would stress that this is not a negotiating team, we just want to make our situation clear to the politicians," he added.
The protest, against government plans to cut drivers' overseas subsistence allowances, was not related to nationwide protests by French truckers.
Tax Minister Carsten Koch on Wednesday offered to shelve cuts and increase the current 150 crown daily allowance to 250 crowns but the drivers insist on at least 500 crowns.
Prusse said the truckers would meet later on Thursday in Padborg to reassess the situation and mull possible new moves.

Some 2,000 Danish drivers have stopped goods traffic from crossing the land border with Germany since Monday, and have since broadened the blockade to most ports, halting exports to Norway, Sweden, Germany, Britain and eastern European countries.
Police said that around 2,000 trucks on Thursday still blocked freight from entering or leaving Denmark at Padborg, but that private cars were being allowed through.
The Danish hauliers' action, combined with the truckers' strike in France has clogged highways and ports and disrupted industry and commerce throughout much of Europe.
Swedish vehicle makers AB Volvo and Saab Auto said that they might have to cut production next week if road haulage chaos continued.

On Wednesday German car manufacturer Volkswagen AG said that the strikes were disrupting production and German air carrier Lufthansa put larger planes on its daily Copenhagen-Frankfurt cargo flight in an effort to partially make up for lost road feeder traffic.

The port blockades hurt not only international trade but also domestic shipments between the main production centres of the Jutland peninsula and Denmark's islands, particularly Zealand where the capital, Copenhagen is located.

Supermarket chains on the island, where about half Denmark's five million people live, warned of food shortages, affecting dairy products, meat and bread in particular, next week if ports remained closed next week.

State-run Danish Radio reported that dairies and meat and fish processing plants throughout the country were increasingly cut off both from sources of raw materials and from markets for finished products and had begun laying off staff.

Trapped at the Padborg border crossing were nearly a million rotting Christmas trees, along with shipments of milk, cheese and meat probably no longer fit for consumption, producers' organisations said.
The Danish post office said international mail and post between the Danish islands and the Jutland peninsula were subject to delays.
